experiments.title: Customer momentum
experiments.summary: Buy suppliers whose major customers just rallied, on the idea that investors are slow to connect a supplier to its customers' news (Cohen & Frazzini 2008).
experiments.takeaway: The lag that shows up across all US stocks didn't appear in the S&P 500, where these links are widely followed.
experiments.hypothesis:
Hypothesis: when a company's major customers have done well, its own stock tends to follow with a delay, because investors are slow to connect a supplier to news about its customers (Cohen & Frazzini 2008, "Economic Links and Predictable Returns"). The reverse should hold when customers do badly. Motivating example: Fabrinet and its customers NVIDIA, Cisco and Amazon.

Data: use the customer_weights data field (view.customer_weights()). It gives each supplier's major customers (10%+ of revenue, from 10-K filings, fiscal 1998 onward) with each customer's share of the supplier's revenue, visible only from 6 months after the supplier's fiscal year-end. Customers are S&P 500 companies only. Shares that were not disclosed are imputed at 10%; keep them by default but expose a parameter to drop them.

Universe: S&P 500 members on the decision date that have at least one visible customer link, raw close at least $5.

Signal: at the last trading session of each month, for each supplier compute the customer return = the revenue-share-weighted average of its visible customers' total returns over the past lookback sessions. Only customers with a finite return count, and the weights are renormalized over them. Use total-return prices.

Entry: buy the suppliers in the top fifth by customer return, equal weight, at the next session's open (market order). If fewer than 5 suppliers qualify, hold cash.

Exit: rebalance monthly; a holding that drops out of the top fifth is sold at the next rebalance. Long-only: when a supplier's customers do badly it is simply not held. No shorting, no stops.

Sizing: equal weight across holdings, total gross exposure 0.95, no leverage.

Parameters: lookback (default 21 sessions, range 10 to 63), top fraction (default 0.2, range 0.1 to 0.33), include_imputed (default true).

What would refute it: no excess return over the S&P 500 after realistic costs in the research period; results that disappear when customer links are shuffled among other companies; or results explained by plain industry momentum (suppliers whose own industry did well) instead of the customer link. Rejecting the idea is an acceptable outcome.
experiments.reason: no version met the targets on research data; the holdout years were left unused

versions.label: Baseline

If customer news diffuses slowly, suppliers ranked high on customer_return outperform other suppliers that have customer links. Simply beating the S&P 500 is not enough, because that can come from universe tilts.

experiments.title: Short-term reversal
experiments.summary: Each week, buy the 20 S&P 500 stocks that fell the most over the past five days and hold them for a week.
experiments.takeaway: Large caps bounce back less than small caps, and weekly turnover gave most of what was left to trading costs.
experiments.hypothesis: Short-term reversal: once a week, rank current S&P 500 members by their return over the past 5 trading days and buy the 20 biggest losers in equal weight at the next open. Hold for one week, then rebalance. Long only. Hypothesis: sharp short-term drops in large, liquid stocks are often overreactions or liquidity-driven selling that partly reverse within days, enough to beat the S&P 500 after trading costs.
experiments.reason: stopped early: all 2 versions were far from the targets (best Sharpe 0.23, target 0.50), so a second round of fixes was not worth running; the holdout years were left unused

versions.label: Baseline

The weekly reversal is a premium for providing liquidity per unit of risk. Ranking by raw ret5 mostly selects high-volatility names whose large moves are normal noise. Ranking by volatility-scaled losses picks stocks that are truly dislocated, and they reverse more per unit of risk.

experiments.title: EWO / RSI indicator signals
experiments.summary: A popular TradingView strategy (Elliott Wave Oscillator plus RSI exhaustion signals), ported to every S&P 500 member, long and short.
experiments.takeaway: Lost money in every variant. The signals look convincing on a chart and show nothing across 500 stocks and 20 years.
experiments.hypothesis: Port of the TradingView strategy 'EWO,RSI advanced Signals Strategy - Exhaustion Filter' v9.4, long/short as in the original, applied to every stock that is an S&P 500 member at each decision date (point-in-time membership) on weekly bars built from daily data (signals at the weekly close, trade at the next open). Per stock: EWO = SMA(hl2,5) - SMA(hl2,34); RSI(close,14); MFI(hlc3,14); vol_ok = weekly volume > 0.8 x SMA(volume,20). oversold_zone becomes true when RSI < 30 and resets to false on a buy. breakout = close > highest high of the previous 10 bars (excluding the current bar). BUY when RSI crosses above 40 and MFI > 30 and EWO > previous EWO and vol_ok and (breakout or oversold_zone). SELL when RSI crosses below 60 and MFI < 70 and EWO < previous EWO and vol_ok. Signals alternate per stock (a buy only after a sell or at start, and vice versa). Go long on BUY and reverse to short on SELL, as the original does (stop-and-reverse: each stock is long, short, or flat before its first signal). No stops or take profits. Portfolio: equal absolute weight across all stocks currently in a position (long or short), at most 5% per stock, gross exposure at most 100% of equity (net is then automatically <= 100%), the rest in cash. Shorts pay Concordance's flat borrow fee. Hypothesis: momentum turning up out of oversold conditions, confirmed by volume and money flow, marks short-to-medium-term bottoms, and the mirror-image SELL marks tops worth shorting; the long/short book should beat the S&P 500 on a risk-adjusted basis.
experiments.reason: stopped early: all 3 versions were far from the targets (best Sharpe -0.29, target 0.50), so a second round of fixes was not worth running; the holdout years were left unused

versions.label: Baseline

If BUY and SELL capture exhaustion reversals over 4–13 weeks, then an event-driven book that holds each fired raw signal for a fixed 8 weeks will earn positive long-minus-short returns. The baseline's permanent, alternation-gated positions mostly hide this.
Exposure older than thirteen weeks dilutes the return contribution of fresh exhaustion signals.

experiments.title: Low volatility + trend filter
experiments.summary: Hold the 50 calmest S&P 500 stocks, and step aside to cash when the index is below its 200-day average.
experiments.takeaway: The only idea to pass every gate and the sealed 2023–2025 holdout (Sharpe 0.74, worst drop −8.8%). The price was return: it trailed a roaring index badly.
experiments.hypothesis: Low-volatility S&P 500 stocks with a market trend filter. At each month-end close, among current S&P 500 members with at least 252 sessions of price history and a raw close of at least 5 dollars, rank stocks by the standard deviation of their daily total returns over the past 252 sessions. Hold the 50 lowest-volatility stocks, equal weight (2% each), long only, rebalanced at the next open after each month-end. Trend filter: build an equal-weighted index of current S&P 500 members from daily total returns; at every close, if that index is below its 200-session simple moving average, the strategy holds no stocks (all cash) from the next open; when it is back above, re-enter the current 50 lowest-volatility names at the next open. No stops, no leverage, no shorts.

versions.label: Baseline
A fixed asymmetric regime band reduces trading enough to improve net Sharpe without materially worsening drawdown.

If the candidate's gain comes from reducing whipsaw in general rather than from the specific 0.97 level, a structurally different hysteresis rule with similar slowness should give similar results. If it does not, the 0.97 result is threshold luck.
The asymmetric filter improves net Sharpe and reduces maximum drawdown relative to the underlying low-volatility sleeve.

headline.label: A fixed asymmetric regime band reduces trading enough to improve net Sharpe without materially worsening drawdown.

experiments.title: Risk-adjusted momentum
experiments.summary: Hold the 25 stocks with the best 12-month return per unit of volatility, and sell when a holding drops out of the top ranks.
experiments.takeaway: Momentum crashes (2003, 2009) kept every version far from the targets.
experiments.hypothesis: Long-only S&P 500 momentum ranked by risk-adjusted return. At each rebalance, score every current S&P 500 member by its trailing return divided by its trailing volatility of daily returns (a Sharpe-style ratio; e.g. 12-month return skipping the most recent month, over 12-month daily volatility). Buy the top-scoring names, equal weight. Hold a name until its score falls below a sell threshold (a buffer looser than the buy cutoff, e.g. it drops out of the top 2x the holding count, or its score falls below a fixed level), then sell it and replace it with the best-ranked name not held. Choose the rebalance frequency (monthly, weekly or daily), the lookback, the number of holdings and the sell threshold yourself, and compare frequencies as separate versions. Use only data known at the decision date.
experiments.reason: no version met the targets on research data; the holdout years were left unused

versions.label: Baseline

The baseline's poor drawdown and high beta come partly from the ratio rewarding high volatility among names with negative momentum. A score that always penalises volatility, regardless of the sign of mom, will select lower-risk names in bear markets without moving to cash.
Forcing positions into nonpositive momentum names weakens continuation and increases losses when positive trends are scarce.

The drawdown and the gap to the benchmark come mainly from momentum crashes during high-volatility regimes. Lowering exposure when the selected portfolio's recent volatility is high, as in Barroso and Santa-Clara's constant-volatility momentum, should raise Sharpe and cut drawdown without changing stock selection.

experiments.title: Calendar-month seasonality
experiments.summary: Long the stocks that have historically done best in the coming calendar month, short those that have done worst (Heston & Sadka 2008).
experiments.takeaway: A well-documented effect in small stocks; in the S&P 500 it was indistinguishable from zero.
experiments.hypothesis: Same-calendar-month return seasonality (Heston & Sadka 2008, JFE; Keloharju, Linnainmaa & Nyberg 2016, JF). At the last close of each month, for every current S&P 500 member, compute a seasonality score: the stock's average total return in the upcoming calendar month over the previous 10 years, using only that same calendar month (month-end to month-end total returns at lags of 12, 24, ..., 120 months, built from tr_close). Require at least 5 of those 10 years; otherwise the stock is not ranked. Rank members by the score. Go long the top quintile and short the bottom quintile, equal weight within each leg, 50% long / 50% short (net 0, gross 1), rebalanced once a month at the next open and held one month. Mechanism: recurring calendar-linked order flow and the timing of earnings announcements and other periodic news (Chang, Hartzmark, Solomon & Soltes 2017) make a stock's return in a given calendar month persist across years. Known risk: the effect may have decayed after publication (2008) and may be offset by seasonal reversals in the other months.
experiments.reason: stopped early: all 3 versions were far from the targets (best Sharpe -0.03, target 0.50), so a second round of fixes was not worth running; the holdout years were left unused

versions.label: Baseline

The predictive content is calendar-specific, meaning a stock does unusually well in month M relative to its own other months. The raw level of its returns adds noise and unrelated exposures. Removing the most recent 12 months from the comparison set avoids loading on short-term reversal and momentum.
A stock's same-month return relative to its own other-month return contains more tradable seasonal information than its raw same-month mean.

experiments.title: Gross profitability
experiments.summary: Hold the most productive fifth of the S&P 500, ranked by gross profit over total assets (Novy-Marx 2013).
experiments.takeaway: Beat the index, but the factor-adjusted alpha wasn't statistically significant (t = 1.8), and it fell 50% in 2008.
experiments.hypothesis: Gross profitability (Novy-Marx 2013, JFE, 'The other side of value: The gross profitability premium'). At the last close of each month, for every current S&P 500 member, compute GP = (trailing-12-month revenue - trailing-12-month cost of goods sold) / total assets, using view.fundamental('revtq_ttm'), view.fundamental('cogsq_ttm') and view.fundamental('atq') (point-in-time Compustat quarterly data; the spec's data_fields must include fundamentals). Only rank stocks with finite GP and total assets > 0. Hold the top quintile by GP, equal weight, fully invested long-only (net 1), rebalanced once a month at the next open. Benchmark: S&P 500. Mechanism: gross profit is the cleanest accounting measure of economic productivity (less polluted by expensed investment such as R&D and advertising), and profitable firms earn higher average returns that investors underprice; Novy-Marx finds the effect is strong among large caps, the opposite of most anomalies. Known risks: it may have decayed after publication (2013); it is a quality/value tilt that can lag in growth-led markets; financial firms cannot be excluded because the view has no industry code.
experiments.reason: no version met the targets on research data; the holdout years were left unused

versions.label: Baseline

If gross profitability itself predicts returns, a top-quintile portfolio weighted by market cap should still beat the cap-weighted S&P 500 on Sharpe and FF5+UMD alpha. If the baseline's edge comes mainly from equal-weighting and its small-cap tilt, value-weighting will remove it.

experiments.title: Value → profitability
experiments.summary: Keep the cheaper half of the S&P 500 by book-to-market, then hold the most profitable fifth of those.
experiments.takeaway: The strongest edge found: +6.1% a year of alpha after six factors (t = 3.3), robust to delaying the accounting data. It failed on risk: −67% in 2008.
experiments.hypothesis: Value + gross profitability, sequential (Novy-Marx 2013, JFE, section on combining profitability and value). At the last close of each month, for every current S&P 500 member: book-to-market BM = view.fundamental('ceqq')[-1] * 1000 / view['mktcap_k'][-1] (ceqq is common equity in $ millions from point-in-time Compustat quarterly data; mktcap_k is CRSP market cap in $ thousands at today's close), and gross profitability GP = (view.fundamental('revtq_ttm') - view.fundamental('cogsq_ttm')) / view.fundamental('atq'), all at the latest row. The spec's data_fields must include fundamentals. Only use stocks with finite BM and GP, ceqq > 0 and atq > 0. Step 1 (filter): keep the cheaper half of eligible members by BM (highest BM). Step 2 (rank): within that half, hold the top quintile by GP (about 50 stocks). This is a sequential filter, not a blended score. Equal weight, fully invested long-only (net 1), rebalanced once a month at the next open. Benchmark: S&P 500. Mechanism: value and profitability are each priced, and they are strongly negatively correlated with each other, so buying cheap stocks that are also productive avoids value traps (cheap because unprofitable) and avoids paying growth prices for quality; Novy-Marx shows the combination roughly doubles the Sharpe of either alone, including among large caps. Known risks: post-publication decay (2013); value had a long drawdown in 2018-2020; financial firms cannot be excluded (no industry code) and banks often have high BM with low GP, so they are mostly removed by the GP step.
experiments.reason: no version met the targets on research data; the holdout years were left unused

versions.label: Baseline

Some of the apparent edge comes from Compustat coverage conventions that silently drop or mis-measure financial firms, whose gross profit and assets are not economically comparable. Excluding firms with an unclassified balance sheet (a supported proxy for banks and insurers) before both sorting steps leaves the strategy's Sharpe ratio and alpha no worse.
The selection signal remains useful when its accounting inputs are delayed by 63 trading sessions.

The baseline's UMD loading of -0.33 is an uncompensated drag and crash source caused by same-day prices pushing recent losers into the cheap half. Removing the weakest momentum names from the cheap half before the GP step will keep the GP-within-value premium and lower the loss from momentum exposure.

experiments.title: Value → profitability, hedged
experiments.summary: The same picks, with an equal-weight basket of the whole S&P 500 shorted against them so that market moves cancel out.
experiments.takeaway: Hedging fixed the crash risk (worst drop −26% instead of −67%), but the alpha shrank to a non-significant +2.5%/yr. In the sealed 2020–2022 holdout it made +2.6%/yr at Sharpe 0.30, short of the 0.5 target.
experiments.hypothesis: Market-hedged version of the sequential value-then-profitability strategy (Novy-Marx 2013, JFE), pre-registered after the long-only version (experiment d378d038) earned a FF5+UMD alpha of +6.1%/yr (t 3.31) but failed only the -35% drawdown gate because of its full market exposure in 2008. At the last close of each month, for every current S&P 500 member: book-to-market BM = view.fundamental('ceqq')[-1] * 1000 / view['mktcap_k'][-1] (ceqq is common equity in $ millions from point-in-time Compustat quarterly data; mktcap_k is CRSP market cap in $ thousands at today's close), and gross profitability GP = (view.fundamental('revtq_ttm') - view.fundamental('cogsq_ttm')) / view.fundamental('atq'), all at the latest row. The spec's data_fields must include fundamentals. Eligible = current members with finite BM and GP, ceqq > 0 and atq > 0. Long leg, unchanged from the long-only version: keep the cheaper half of eligible members by BM (highest BM), then within that half hold the top quintile by GP (about 50 stocks), equal weight summing to +1.0. This is a sequential filter, not a blended score. Hedge leg: short an equal-weight basket of ALL eligible members summing to -1.0 (each about -1/N). A stock in both legs gets the sum of its two weights. Net exposure 0, gross about 2. Rebalanced once a month at the next open; shorts pay the default borrow fee. The hedge is a fixed rule, not tuned: it is not beta-scaled, not timed, and not a subset of stocks. Benchmark: S&P 500, but the point of the test is the spread between the picks and the average member. Mechanism: value and profitability are each priced and negatively correlated with each other, so cheap-and-productive stocks avoid value traps; hedging with the equal-weight universe removes the market (and most of the size tilt) and leaves the selection edge. Known risks: post-publication decay (2013); value's long drawdown in 2018-2020; financial firms cannot be excluded by industry code; the hedge leg trades about 500 names a month, so costs matter.

versions.label: Baseline

Part of the shortfall comes from cheap, high-GP names in persistent decline (falling knives), which give the -0.25 UMD loading. Removing the worst intermediate-momentum names from L raises raw return. It also raises FF5+UMD alpha only if those names carry negative idiosyncratic return beyond their UMD exposure.

The momentum screen's negative alpha comes mostly from periods with a short-only book (L empty or MOM unavailable), not from the screen itself. If the book is forced flat whenever there is no long leg, the screened strategy's FF5+UMD alpha is at least the baseline's.
An empty momentum-screen long set creates unintended directional short exposure that confounds the intended long-short experiment.

experiments.title: Net share issuance
experiments.summary: Long the S&P 500 stocks that shrank their share count most over 12 months (buybacks), short the heaviest issuers. Market-neutral.
experiments.takeaway: Made 3.4% a year at Sharpe 0.35, but the edge was just the investment and profitability factors in disguise: alpha after six factors was −1.8%/yr. Rejected before the holdout, which stays unused.
experiments.hypothesis: Net share issuance, long/short (Pontiff & Woodgate 2008, JF, 'Share Issuance and Cross-sectional Returns'; Daniel & Titman 2006; Fama & French 2008, JF, 'Dissecting Anomalies', who find net stock issues predict returns in all size groups including big stocks). At the last close of each month, for every current S&P 500 member with 253 sessions of history, compute 12-month net issuance ISS = log(mktcap_k[t] / mktcap_k[t-252]) - sum over the same 252 sessions of log(1 + retx), where retx is the price-only (ex-dividend, split-adjusted) return. This is the log change in split-adjusted shares outstanding: positive = net issuer (equity offerings, stock-financed acquisitions, employee stock), negative = net repurchaser. Require finite mktcap at both ends and finite retx on every session in the window; skip names failing that. Sort eligible members into quintiles by ISS. Long the lowest quintile (biggest net repurchasers) in equal weight summing to +1.0; short the highest quintile (biggest net issuers) in equal weight summing to -1.0. Net exposure 0, gross 2. Rebalance monthly at the next open; shorts pay the default borrow fee. This is a sorted long/short, not a blended score; quintile breakpoints, the 252-session window and the 1.0/1.0 leg sizes are fixed, not tuned. Benchmark: S&P 500, but the test is the spread between the legs. Mechanism: managers have private information and time the market, issuing equity when it is overvalued and repurchasing when it is undervalued, and investors underreact to these signals (Loughran & Ritter 1995 on post-issue underperformance; Ikenberry, Lakonishok & Vermaelen 1995 on post-buyback drift). Known risks: overlap with the investment (CMA) and profitability (RMW) factors, so judge alpha against FF5 + momentum; stock-financed mergers create large one-off issuance; post-publication decay; repurchasers lean value, so 2018-2020 value weakness may hurt.
experiments.reason: no version met the targets on research data; the holdout years were left unused

versions.label: Baseline
The issuance ranking retains useful predictive information when its newest 63 sessions are excluded.

experiments.title: Quality + cash-flow sleeves
experiments.summary: Five market-neutral sleeves (asset turnover, return on operating assets, ROE, gross profitability, free-cash-flow yield), each long the top fifth and short the bottom fifth of the S&P 500. Chosen on pre-2017 published evidence.
experiments.takeaway: The first idea to pass the published-evidence check, and it still fell short: +2.5% a year at Sharpe 0.32, with alpha after six factors of +1.6% (t 1.1). Real but small, and well below the published mega-cap numbers once costs and an S&P-only universe are applied.
experiments.hypothesis: Five market-neutral factor sleeves combined in equal shares, chosen on published mega-cap evidence available before 2017 (Jensen, Kelly & Pedersen 2023 factor library: each was still earning a mega-cap long/short Sharpe of 0.35-0.75 after its original paper's sample, through 2016; book-to-market and low volatility were excluded as dead by the same test). This is a portfolio of five separate single-signal sleeves, not a blended score. At the last close of each month, for every current S&P 500 member, compute from point-in-time quarterly Compustat via view.fundamental (the spec's data_fields must include fundamentals) and CRSP: book enterprise value BEV = ceqq + dlttq + dlcq + pstkq - cheq, treating a missing dlttq, dlcq, pstkq or cheq as 0 but requiring ceqq. Signals, all at the latest row: (1) asset turnover = saleq_ttm / BEV, (2) return on net operating assets = oiadpq_ttm / BEV, both only where BEV > 0; (3) quarterly return on equity = ibq / ceqq, only where ceqq > 0; (4) gross profitability = (revtq_ttm - cogsq_ttm) / atq, only where atq > 0; (5) free-cash-flow yield = (oancfq_ttm - capxq_ttm) * 1000 / mktcap_k (fundamentals are in $ millions, mktcap_k in $ thousands). Each sleeve ranks the members with a finite value of its own signal: long the top quintile in equal weight summing to +0.2, short the bottom quintile in equal weight summing to -0.2. Add the five sleeves' weights per stock (a stock can appear in several sleeves; opposite positions net). Net exposure 0, gross at most 2. Rebalance monthly at the next open; shorts pay the default borrow fee. Quintiles, the five signals, the equal 0.2 sleeve shares and the formulas are fixed, not tuned. Benchmark: S&P 500, but the test is the market-neutral spread. Mechanism: investors underprice durable profitability and efficient use of capital and overpay for unprofitable 'junk' (Novy-Marx 2013; Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen 2019 'Quality minus junk'), and free cash flow is a cash-based value measure less exposed to accounting distortions than book value. Combining five related but distinct sleeves diversifies each signal's noise. Known risks: all five are quality/profitability tilts and are correlated, so diversification is limited; they load on the RMW profitability factor, so judge alpha against FF5 + momentum and expect much of the return to be RMW; financial firms cannot be excluded by industry code, and their BEV-based ratios are noisy; post-publication decay.
experiments.reason: no version met the targets on research data; the holdout years were left unused

versions.label: Baseline

Cross-sleeve netting wastes gross exposure and cancels positions, reducing the signal's information. A composite that ranks on agreement across signals will concentrate gross in consistently high- or low-quality names, lifting net Sharpe at the same or lower turnover.
Zero-filling unavailable BEV components contaminates S1 and S2 rankings enough to reduce their net contribution.

Dividing S1 and S2 by BEV creates a growth (negative-HML) bet and lets tiny-book firms that buy back heavily dominate the extremes. That reduces alpha and cancels against S5. Dividing by total assets instead, as Novy-Marx does, measures operating efficiency without the book-size distortion.

experiments.title: Futures TSMOM (Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen), 1975–
experiments.hypothesis: Time-series momentum across all available futures markets, Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen style. For each market, go long if its trailing 12-month excess return is positive and short if negative. Size each market to target 40%/N annualized volatility using an exponentially weighted 60-day volatility estimate (N = number of markets with data). Rebalance monthly at the next open. Cap total portfolio volatility at 15% annualized. Controls to compare against: equal-risk buy-and-hold of the same markets, equity-index-only TSMOM, and a random-sign placebo. Also report correlation with the S&P 500 and returns during the stock market's worst months.
